newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa faces flat gold output in 97.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa faces flat gold output in 97.

text.p: Forecasts from the biggest gold producer of a flat output in 1997 suggest South Africa as whole may once again struggle to produce 500 tonnes this year.
Chamber of Mines economist Roger Baxter said on Thursday he expected final 1996 production to come in around 494 to 495 tonnes from 522.4 tonnes in 1995, with output in 1997 likely to be similar.
"It varies from group to group, but on an aggregate basis we anticipate that production is going to go sideways at around 500 tonnes," he said.

"We're not going to see another 30-tonne drop like we saw last year, but there are no big increases in the foreseeable future -- though we are going to see replacement tonnage shafts coming through. Stabilisation and consolidation is the name of the game."
Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd -- which accounts for more than 40 percent of South African production -- said earlier it expected a flat 1997 gold output.
The world's largest gold producer said its mines should produce 213.2 tonnes in 1997 against 212.8 in 1996 (corrects figures).
It said Free State Consolidated Gold Mines Ltd was likely to see output fall in 1997 to 78 from 83.4 tonnes.
Official national output figures for 1996 will be published early next month. In the 11 months to November, production was 450.6 tonnes, a 5.7 percent decline on the year ago period.
Gold production in South Africa, the world biggest producer of the yellow metal, has been dropping steadily in the past decade due to increasing costs and decreasing recovery grades.
The 1996 production year promises to be the worst since 1956 with output half that produced in 1970.
South Africa's gold mines are the deepest in the world, with some reaching over three kilometres underground, making gold recovery very expensive and dangerous.
But the country still holds around 40 percent of the world's identified gold reserves and despite the high costs and a low gold price at present the industry is continuing to invest in new projects.
Anglo American said last year it was investigating two new ultra deep mines which could see gold mined up to five kilometres below the earth's surface.
